evals.prompt: Use the synthetic flattened logo fixture at evals/files/flattened-logo.png. Make a tasteful 4-second white-background animation: the emblem should establish first, the wordmark should enter while the emblem is still readable, and the final state must match the source. I also need a checkpoint sheet and a high-resolution output plan. Do not pretend the flattened file contains independent letters or leaves.
evals.expected_output: The agent identifies the flattened-source limitation, requests or records approved groups, creates a renderer-neutral brief/manifest with 120 frames at 30 fps by default, uses a whole-mark or approved-group fallback, and specifies final-state/QA checks.
assertions: The response explicitly classifies the source as flattened or otherwise non-semantic.
The response does not claim that connected components are guaranteed independent logo layers.
The response records 120 frames at 30 fps when using the four-second default.
The response includes a final hold, reduced-motion behavior, and a final-state acceptance check.
The response requests a checkpoint/contact sheet and documents the flattened-source limitation.

evals.prompt: Use the layered fixture at evals/files/layered-mark.svg for our education startup. We need a clean geometric/botanical reveal for a website and a 9:16 social version, without generic neon AI effects. The mark should assemble or unfold into the approved lockup. Explain what source layers, pivots, timing, and delivery variants you need before rendering.
evals.expected_output: The agent classifies the vector/layered source, selects one restrained primary pattern, names the required semantic layers and pivots, proposes separate square and vertical compositions from one timing model, and avoids inventing geometry or effects.
assertions: The response identifies the SVG as vector/layered source rather than a flattened raster.
The response selects one primary motion pattern and no more than two supporting gestures.
The response requests or records semantic pivots, z-order, and exact text outlines.
The response includes square and 9:16 output planning with separate canvases.
The response excludes generic neon/AI effects unless justified by the brand.

evals.prompt: We only have a flattened logo PNG and need a transparent looping animation for a product header. Can you make the letters and a ring animate independently, and deliver a dotLottie or WebM? Include reduced-motion behavior and tell me what is impossible from the flattened source.
evals.expected_output: The agent separates alpha/white/opaque delivery, explains that independent motion and hidden pixels are blocked without layers, proposes a grouped or whole-mark fallback, defines loop-boundary and reduced-motion checks, and avoids promising a dotLottie/WebM before the source and runtime are confirmed.
assertions: The response distinguishes transparent, white, and opaque outputs.
The response marks independent letters/ring motion as blocked or provisional from a flattened source.
The response requests vector/layered source or an approved reconstruction.
The response includes loop first/last-state and reduced-motion requirements.
The response does not silently fabricate hidden detail or claim that a runtime format is universally supported.

evals.prompt: Review the motion manifest at evals/files/invalid-motion-spec.json. Identify why it should not render, then produce a corrected manifest using the supplied layered fixture and explain the final-state acceptance criteria.
evals.expected_output: The agent runs or applies the manifest validator, catches frame ordering, bounds, easing, scale, and noncanonical-final-transform errors, repairs the manifest, and explains encoded-output tolerance separately from canonical geometry.
assertions: The response identifies the invalid frame ordering and invalid bounds.
The response identifies the unsupported easing token and nonpositive scale.
The corrected manifest passes the bundled validator.
The response requires a static hold and canonical final transform for final-state layers.
The response distinguishes exact canonical geometry from codec-tolerant RGB comparison.
